scope: Research-only staging. No canonical/public mutation or evidence-grade promotion.

entries.finding: A 17-trial meta-analysis found garlic intake lowered systolic blood pressure by about 3.75 mm Hg versus control; this is pooled preparation-level evidence, not proof for every garlic product.
The same meta-analysis found a pooled diastolic blood-pressure reduction of about 3.39 mm Hg, with greater heterogeneity than the systolic analysis.
In subgroup analysis, systolic blood pressure fell significantly in hypertensive participants but not in normotensive participants; the population boundary should remain explicit.
The pooled subgroup analysis did not show a significant systolic blood-pressure reduction among normotensive participants, providing counterevidence against a universal BP-lowering claim.

A 16-trial systematic review/meta-analysis found inorganic nitrate or beetroot juice was associated with a roughly 4.4 mm Hg reduction in systolic blood pressure versus placebo in short-duration crossover trials.
The 2013 beetroot/nitrate meta-analysis did not find a statistically significant pooled reduction in diastolic blood pressure, despite the systolic signal.

Meta-regression in the beetroot/nitrate review found an association between daily inorganic-nitrate dose and systolic blood-pressure change, but the included interventions were short and heterogeneous.

A systematic review/meta-analysis of seven randomized trials in adults with arterial hypertension found nitrate-rich beetroot juice reduced systolic blood pressure by about 4.95 mm Hg; intervention durations ranged from 3 to 60 days.

In adults with arterial hypertension, nitrate-derived beetroot juice did not significantly reduce diastolic blood pressure in the pooled analysis, so the evidence should not be summarized as uniform BP lowering.
An updated dose-response meta-analysis of 24 randomized trials in type 2 diabetes found cinnamon supplementation significantly reduced fasting blood sugar versus control.

The same 24-RCT meta-analysis found a statistically significant reduction in HbA1c with cinnamon supplementation, while emphasizing the need to interpret heterogeneous preparations and trial designs cautiously.
Pooled insulin concentration did not change significantly in the updated cinnamon meta-analysis, providing an important counterweight to broader claims of improved insulin physiology.

An umbrella meta-analysis of prior interventional meta-analyses found conflicting conclusions across cinnamon glycemic syntheses, reinforcing that preparation, population, endpoint and meta-analysis quality must be retained rather than collapsed into one efficacy label.

A 2025-2026 updated meta-analysis of 26 randomized controlled trials found fenugreek seed significantly reduced fasting blood glucose, but heterogeneity was substantial and higher-quality confirmation was recommended.

The updated fenugreek meta-analysis found a significant reduction in 2-hour postprandial glucose, with very high heterogeneity across trials; this should remain a pooled signal rather than a preparation-independent effect.
Fenugreek supplementation significantly reduced HbA1c in the 26-RCT synthesis, while the authors called for higher-quality trials to confirm the result.
The updated fenugreek meta-analysis did not find a statistically significant HOMA-IR effect, so glucose reductions should not automatically be translated into improved insulin resistance.

An earlier meta-analysis found glucose reductions were most evident in trials using medium or high fenugreek doses among people with diabetes, while substantial heterogeneity remained; dose and disease status therefore matter.

A systematic review/meta-analysis of clinical trials found cranberry products reduced urinary-tract-infection incidence versus controls, with a pooled risk ratio of about 0.68; this is prevention evidence, not treatment of an active UTI.
In a 2012 systematic review of randomized trials, cranberry products were associated with lower UTI risk among women with recurrent UTIs, while substantial heterogeneity across studies remained.
A 2024 network meta-analysis of 20 trials found cranberry juice was associated with fewer UTIs than placebo liquid and no treatment; product form and comparator must remain explicit.

A meta-analysis of 10 randomized trials reported that cranberry products providing at least 36 mg/day of proanthocyanidins were associated with a modestly lower UTI risk, supporting a dose/composition boundary rather than a generic cranberry equivalence claim.

A 2019 systematic review/meta-analysis found a lower risk of upper-respiratory infection with Echinacea preparations, but clinical heterogeneity, selective reporting and varied preparations limited certainty and clinical interpretation.
The 2019 Echinacea synthesis did not find convincing evidence that Echinacea shortened upper-respiratory infection duration, providing counterevidence against a broad cold-treatment claim.

A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials involving 180 participants reported reduced upper-respiratory symptom severity with black elderberry supplementation, but the small total evidence base limits confidence and does not establish treatment of influenza or other specific infections.
